orbit-types.problem: how orbit shape, plane orientation and period combine to determine a satellite’s path in space and its subpoint on Earth.
explanation: The two upper views and the map follow the same satellite at the same instant. The spatial view shows an orbit tilted relative to Earth’s spin axis, while the orbit-plane view removes that viewing angle so the ellipse is easy to recognize. Earth is at a focus. Semimajor axis a is measured from Earth’s center and fixes the two-body period T = 2π√(a³/μ); eccentricity e controls the shape. Perigee and apogee altitudes are hp = a(1 − e) − RE and ha = a(1 + e) − RE. Altitude h excludes Earth’s radius RE; geocentric radius r includes it.

Mean anomaly M = nt advances uniformly with time, with n = √(μ/a³). Solving M = E − e sin E gives eccentric anomaly E and the orbital position. The satellite moves faster near perigee and dwells longer near apogee. Equal-time dots reveal that difference. Inclination i tilts the orbital plane: i = 0° is equatorial prograde, i = 90° is polar, and i > 90° is retrograde. Ω rotates the ascending-node direction around the spin axis; ω rotates perigee within the orbital plane. The apsis slider adds Δω to the preset’s ω. A circular orbit has no unique perigee, and an equatorial orbit has no unique ascending node, even though a coordinate phase and orientation can still be chosen.

The ground track is the latitude and longitude of the point directly beneath the satellite on a rotating spherical Earth. Transform the inertial position by the opposite Earth-rotation angle before finding longitude. Inclination sets the latitude range; period and Earth rotation set the longitude shift between passes. A sidereal period alone makes an orbit geosynchronous. Keeping one fixed subpoint additionally requires a circular, equatorial, prograde orbit: GEO. Inclined or eccentric geosynchronous cases move across the map while repeating after a sidereal day. LEO and MEO describe altitude ranges; polar and retrograde describe orientation, so these categories can overlap.

Tundra-like and Molniya-like ellipses illustrate high-latitude dwell. The supplied ω = 270° places apogee north; rotating the apsides can move it south or toward the equator. The Tundra-like period is one sidereal day; Molniya-like is half a sidereal day, so its two daily apogees alternate longitudes before the complete track repeats. Their approximately 63.4° inclination is associated with canceling first-order secular J2 drift of the argument of perigee. This fixed-element two-body demonstration omits J2 and all other perturbations. The map shows a subpoint, not an observer’s azimuth–elevation sky track or a coverage boundary. Coastlines are schematic, and each preset refits the spatial scale.
orbit-types.example: Using μ = 398,600.4418 km³/s² and RE = 6,378.137 km, a circular orbit at 500 km altitude has a = 6,878.137 km and a period of about 94.6 minutes. A geostationary orbit instead matches the 86,164.0905 s sidereal day, giving a ≈ 42,164 km and h ≈ 35,786 km. The same circular shape can therefore have very different period and altitude.

questions.prompt: The period remains one sidereal day while inclination changes from 0° to 30°, with eccentricity still zero. Which aspects of the ground track and altitude change?
questions.hint: Separate orbital size and shape from orientation, and compare the GEO and inclined-geosynchronous presets.
questions.answer: Semimajor axis and constant circular altitude stay the same because the period and eccentricity stay the same. The subpoint now moves north and south, and its Earth-fixed longitude also varies over the orbit. The track repeats each sidereal day, but the satellite is no longer geostationary.

questions.prompt: Why do equal-time dots crowd near apogee on an eccentric orbit, and what happens to the apogee hemisphere if Δω changes by 180°?
questions.hint: Use angular-momentum conservation and the meaning of a rotation within the orbital plane.
questions.answer: At greater radius the satellite moves more slowly, so equal time intervals cover less distance near apogee. Rotating the apsides by 180° exchanges their directions within the plane, moving a northern apogee to the corresponding southern latitude while leaving eccentricity and period unchanged.
